title: Voiced S-Row — ざ じ ず ぜ ぞ

points.name: ざ
points.explanation: The syllable ざ is the voiced version of さ — add a dakuten to さ and the 's' becomes a 'z', producing a 'za' sound as in 'pizza' or 'zebra'. Your vocal cords buzz for 'z' but not for 's'. ざ appears in useful vocabulary like ざっし (magazine — though the small っ will be covered soon), ごみばこ, and the borrowing ざ used in theater terms. More importantly for grammar, ざ shows up in negative verb endings like 〜ざるをえない ('cannot but / must'). The character ざ looks identical to さ but with two small strokes added to the upper right.
rules: ざ = さ + dakuten; voiced 'z' before 'ah'.
Test voicing: put your hand on your throat. さ = no buzz; ざ = buzz.
The character ざ is visually identical to さ except for the two small dakuten strokes.

examples.english: cold buckwheat noodles on a bamboo strainer

points.flashcardAnswer: za — like the 'za' in 'pizza' (voiced version of さ)

points.name: じ
points.explanation: The syllable じ is the voiced version of し, and just as し is pronounced 'shi' rather than 'si', じ is pronounced 'ji' rather than 'zi'. It produces the 'j' sound in 'jeans' or 'measure' — a voiced palatal fricative. じ is one of the most common sounds in Japanese and appears in essential vocabulary: じかん (time), じしん (earthquake / self-confidence), じぶん (oneself), and the particle じゃ (a contraction of では, meaning 'well then'). You'll encounter じ constantly in both spoken and written Japanese.
rules: じ = し + dakuten; always pronounced 'ji' (like 'jeans'), never 'zi'.
じかん (time) and じぶん (oneself) are extremely high-frequency vocabulary words.
じゃ is a contraction of では, used constantly: じゃまた (see you!) / じゃあね (bye!).
points.flashcardAnswer: ji — like 'jeans' (voiced version of し; always 'ji', never 'zi')

points.name: ず
points.explanation: The syllable ず is the voiced version of す — 'z' before the Japanese unrounded 'u' vowel. It sounds like 'zu' but with flat, unrounded lips (not like English 'zoo', which rounds the lips). ず appears in みず (water — one of the most essential Japanese nouns!), かず (number / count), and the common verb ending ず, which is a formal/literary negative form. The word みず (water) is probably the most important word featuring ず and one of the first nouns every learner picks up.
rules: ず = す + dakuten; voiced 'z' before the flat, unrounded Japanese 'u'.
Don't round lips for ず — keep them flat like Japanese 'u'.
みず (water) is essential vocabulary — one of the most frequent nouns in Japanese.
points.flashcardAnswer: zu — voiced 'z' + Japanese 'u' (flat lips; not like 'zoo')

points.name: ぜ
points.explanation: The syllable ぜ is the voiced version of せ — 'z' before the 'eh' vowel, sounding like 'ze' as in 'zest' or 'zen'. ぜ appears in vocabulary like ぜんぶ (all / everything), ぜったい (absolutely / definitely), and the loanword ぜろ (zero). ぜんぶ is an especially useful word that you'll reach for constantly when describing totals or completeness. The sentence-final particle ぜ (informal, mostly male speech) adds strong assertion — similar to the even more emphatic ぞ.
rules: ぜ = せ + dakuten; voiced 'z' before 'eh'.
ぜんぶ (all/everything) and ぜったい (absolutely) are high-frequency words.
ぜ as a sentence-final particle (informal male speech) expresses strong assertion.
points.flashcardAnswer: ze — like the 'ze' in 'zest' (voiced version of せ)

points.name: ぞ
points.explanation: The syllable ぞ is the voiced version of そ — 'z' before the 'oh' vowel, like the start of 'zone' or 'zombie'. ぞ appears in ぞう (elephant), ぞうきん (cleaning rag), and the common expression それがぞ! (informal emphatic). Like ぜ, the sentence-final particle ぞ carries strong, emphatic assertion — stronger than ぜ and typically used in energetic, informal (often male) speech. ぞ also appears in the fascinating word ぞっとする (to shudder / to feel a chill) — one of those evocative onomatopoeic expressions Japanese does so well.
rules: ぞ = そ + dakuten; voiced 'z' before 'oh'.
ぞ as a sentence-final particle expresses strong, emphatic assertion (informal male speech).
ぞう (elephant) is a great beginner vocabulary word featuring ぞ.
points.flashcardAnswer: zo — like the 'zo' in 'zone' (voiced version of そ)

chapterPractice.prompt: What sound does じ make? (Hint: it's the voiced version of し)
chapterPractice.explanation: じ makes the 'ji' sound (like 'jeans'), not 'zi'. Just as し is always 'shi' not 'si', its voiced version じ is always 'ji'. This is consistent with the し irregularity.

chapterPractice.prompt: Which character is the voiced version of す?
chapterPractice.explanation: ず is the voiced version of す. Add dakuten (゛) to す → ず. The 's' sound becomes a voiced 'z', with flat, unrounded lips for the 'u' vowel.
みず (mizu) means 'water'. み (mi) + ず (zu) = mizu. One of the most fundamental nouns in Japanese — you'll need this word from day one!
かぞく (kazoku) means 'family'. か (ka) + ぞ (zo) + く (ku) = kazoku. Notice how ぞ (voiced そ) appears in this everyday word.
